In a 25-minute run of our Rust prototype, six nodes converged on identical trees and difficulty targets, and 65% of slots were filled against 63% predicted. In simulation with delays of 5% of the lane interval, a single chain at the same block rate wasted 1.7 to 3.3 times as much work as 2 to 8 lanes, although nodes more often held later-discarded blocks. Among Bitcoin transactions whose spent scripts could be rebuilt, about 95% kept their inputs in one lane, mostly because they spend a single output.

item.title: Homomorphism in Expectation: Leveled Homomorphic Encryption with Range-Relative Correctness
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2854
Authors: Zeyu Liu, Xianhui Lu, Ruida Wang, Xinxuan Zhang
Summary: Lattices have dominated the development of homomorphic encryption for deep computation. We introduce $\textit{Homomorphism in Expectation (HIE)}$, a new construction showing that encrypted addition suffices for both addition and multiplication in deep real-valued computation.
Given any additively homomorphic encryption scheme over $\mathbb{Z}_2$, we construct range-relatively correct leveled homomorphic encryption for arithmetic circuits $C$ of $\textit{arbitrary}$ polynomial depth. For depth bound $d$ and any chosen public input bound $r>0$, our scheme supports inputs in $[-r,r]$. Outputs lie in $[-\eta_C,\eta_C]$, where $\eta_C=C(r,\ldots,r)$ is the circuit's maximum output range magnitude over this input range. Decryption returns an answer with error at most $\varepsilon\cdot\eta_C$ except with probability $\delta$. Each input requires $\ell_{\mathsf{in}}=O(d+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ base ciphertexts, and each output requires $\ell_{\mathsf{out}}=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ base ciphertexts. For $n$ inputs, online evaluation uses only ${\sim}\ell_{\mathsf{out}}\cdot n\cdot\ell_{\mathsf{in}}$ ciphertext additions and ${\sim}\ell_{\mathsf{out}}\cdot |C|\cdot\ell_{\mathsf{in}}$ memory accesses.
Our construction begins by encoding real-valued inputs as encrypted bitstreams, allowing multiplication through encrypted bit addition. The direct approach incurs costs exponential in circuit depth, limiting efficient evaluation to logarithmic depth and requiring non-compact input ciphertexts. We overcome these limitations with new encoding and circuit evaluation techniques, which eliminate the exponential overhead, enabling compact homomorphic arithmetic at arbitrary polynomial depth from additive encryption alone.

item.title: ASCENT: Algebraic Structured Compilation of Exact Norms for Succinct Lattice Proofs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2853
Authors: Lizhen Zhang, Shang Gao, Bin Xiao
Summary: Norm bounds are semantic constraints in lattice cryptography: satisfying the modular equations is not enough unless the witness also satisfies the prescribed shortness bound. Existing norm reductions either introduce slack, or rely on general sumcheck style machinery whose transcript cost grows with the witness length. We introduce a reduction-of-knowledge compiler for exact $\ell_2$-norm constraints. It compiles the original norm language for a committed lattice witness into a narrow structured relation consisting only of commitment-opening constraints, tensor-structured witness-public inner-product claims, and relaxed admissible shortness bounds. Exact norm soundness is enforced inside the reduction, so the remaining proof obligation is structured and algebraic.
The compiler adds only $O(1)$ prover-to-verifier communication, measured in ring and field elements, independent of the witness length $N$, and requires only $O(\log N)$ verifier work. The same techniques can also extend to a folding mechanism for broader quadratic relations, including R1CS-type circuits. At $128$-bit security, our concrete estimates give transcripts of about $27.69\mathrm{KB}$ for exact norm reduction and $27.75\mathrm{KB}$ for the R1CS folding application. This is about $3$--$4\times$ smaller than LatticeFold+, about $2$--$3\times$ smaller than SALSAA, and remains close to the compact estimates reported for Cyclo.

item.title: A Tutorial on Oblivious Random Access Memory
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2852
Authors: Elaine Shi, Srinivas Devadas
Summary: Abstract—Oblivious RAM (ORAM) is a key technique for pro- tecting memory access patterns in systems with untrusted mem- ory, including secure processors, trusted execution environments, and multi-party computation. This article presents a tutorial overview of ORAM concepts and designs from an algorithmic and cryptographic perspective. We review the security goals and threat models underlying ORAM, describe the most popular ORAM constructions and their core mechanisms, and discuss practical considerations for implementing ORAM. The tutorial aims to provide readers with a clear foundation for understanding ORAM-based memory protection and its applications.

item.title: Bounding the security of the Bromberg-Shpilrain-Vdovina hash function
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2851
Authors: Eilidh McKemmie
Summary: The Bromberg-Shpilrain-Vdovina hash functions are a family of Cayley hash functions indexed by an integer parameter $k\ge 2$. Hashes are matrices in $SL_2(p)$ where $p$ is a large prime. We present an attack which finds collisions of length $O(\log p)$ whose average-case time complexity is $O(p^{0.28})$ when $k=2$ and $O(p^{0.36})$ when $k=3$ under an assumption in the spirit of Zaremba's Conjecture on continued fractions. This is an improvement on the more general attacks of Mullan-Tsaban and Slaughter which have average-case time complexity $O(\sqrt{p})$. For any $k$, the average-case time complexity of our attack is $O(p^{1-\delta_k+o(1)})$ where $\delta_k$ is the Hausdorff dimension of a certain Cantor set. This tends to $O(\sqrt{p})$ as $k\to\infty$, so our attack has time complexity comparable to Mullan-Tsaban and Slaughter's attacks as $k$ grows. We give examples of collisions for large primes found by our attack when $k=2, 3$.

item.title: Neural Cipher Bench: Cost and Portability of Corner-ReLU Cipher Implementation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2850
Authors: Siwoo Eum, Minwoo Lee, Gyeongju Song, Seungwon Lee, Uijae Kim, Doyun Park, Minseo Kim, Wai Kong Lee, Zhe Liu, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Hwajeong Seo
Summary: Edge and Internet of Things (IoT) devices run neural networks on GPUs, neural processing units (NPUs), and microcontrollers (MCUs) through machine learning (ML) runtimes. Deep Neural Cryptography (DNC, EUROCRYPT 2026) expressed AES as a bit-exact ReLU network with fixed weights, using a corner-ReLU construction that keeps the cipher inside the affine+ReLU operators such runtimes execute. What this construction costs on edge and IoT hardware, and whether real ML backends execute it correctly, had not been measured. We implement SM4, ARIA, Camellia, and ChaCha20 (spanning substitution–permutation, Feistel, and add–rotate–XOR structures) alongside AES on a shared corner-ReLU core under one construction policy, derive a cost model for width, depth, and neuron count, and measure five execution paths on four platforms. All ciphers admit bit-exact networks whose width and depth diverge with cipher structure, and the model's width predicted where GPU throughput drops. Every configuration passing the correctness check fell below its classical baseline (best 0.80×, SM4 on the GPU), by hundreds to thousands of times for the S-box ciphers on the MCU, and keeping the activations on chip through fusion raised throughput 1.4–3.5× and moved the peak past the predicted cache limit without closing the gap. Some AES configurations on the Apple Neural Engine returned valid-looking but incorrect outputs with no error or warning, a failure reproduced in a minimal graph without project code. Mathematical bit-exactness therefore does not guarantee backend-level bit-exactness, and exact workloads offloaded to edge NPUs require output validation.

item.title: TUTTI: Parallel CKKS Bootstrapping in under 3 ms on CPU
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2848
Authors: Robin Köstler, Antonio Guimarães
Summary: This paper introduces TUTTI, a new CKKS bootstrapping procedure that outperforms previous low-latency solutions in multi-threaded latency for any number of messages and, most notably, has a lower latency than TFHE when bootstrapping a single one. Our bootstrapping builds upon SPRU (CK, TCHES 2027), improving it with new methods for exploiting parallelism and increasing the number of messages, as well as with a refined security analysis, of independent interest, of the block-binary secret keys of LMSS (AsiaCCS 2023). \tutti bootstraps $4096$ real-number messages in $46$ to $83.4$ ms on $192$ threads to restore $1$ to $9$ multiplicative levels, outperforming SHIP (CHKS, Eurocrypt 2025) by a factor of up to $3$ on the same machine. Unlike SHIP, TUTTI gains immediately from bootstrapping fewer messages, with a $256$-message bootstrapping taking just $15$ to $34$ ms on $32$ threads. For a single message, TUTTI takes $4.6$ ms on $32$ threads, whereas TFHE-rs needs $7.3$ ms for a $4$-bit bootstrapping on the same machine and thread count. We show that this advantage persists across different architectures: on an Apple M5 Pro laptop (ARM), TUTTI takes $2.4$ ms on $14$ threads, against $4.5$ ms for TFHE-rs. Differences between CKKS and lightweight schemes such as TFHE remain on several fronts, from functionality to key sizes and security assumptions, but our work shows that multi-threaded latency is no longer one of them, closing a long-standing gap in the practical FHE literature.

item.title: Access Cost Tradeoffs in Mixed-Mode Oblivious RAM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2847
Authors: Wojciech Ciszewski, Emanuele Ragnoli
Summary: A mixed-mode oblivious RAM (ORAM) lets each memory request be marked public or private: public requests disclose their addresses, private requests hide them. We ask how much work such a scheme must do, and which requests must do it, in the cell-probe model—with a passive server that only reads and overwrites addressed words. We examine the expected amortized per-request cost on randomized workloads with independent modes and uniformly random addresses. For array size $n$ and client memory $m\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$ words, let $H=\log_2(2+n/(m+1))$.
Our main result is a tight tradeoff between the cost of public reads and private writes. We show that if a request is private with probability $0<p\le1/2$ and private requests cost at most $Q$ probes on average, then every scheme with $m\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$ has expected public-read cost\[ \Omega\!\left(\max\left\{1, \frac{H}{\log_2(2+1/p+Q/H)}\right\}\right), \]even when the server learns the kind (read/write) of each private request. For polynomial $m$, we provide constructions that match this bound whenever $Q$ exceeds a threshold that we identify for both $Q$ treated as an expectation over the workload and as the average cost for the worst-case workload. In particular, at constant private frequency $p$ a logarithmic private budget forces logarithmic public-read cost, and constant public-read cost requires private cost $(n/(m+1))^{\Omega(1)}$. This answers, for passive servers, the question posed by Zhang, Wang, and Weng, whose PIR-based scheme achieves constant public and logarithmic private bandwidth with server computation. Our lower bound proof fixes the public query and changes its private history; crucially, we charge them separately. Our constructions combine a public cache with linear merges of hash tables.
Two further groups of results concern public writes and total work. Firstly, we give a cost tradeoff between public writes and private reads. Secondly, for workloads mixing private operations, public reads, and public writes with probabilities $p,r,a$, we show that every scheme with $m\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$ has total cost per request $\Omega(\max\{1,H/\log_2(2+1/p)\})$ when private request kinds are hidden, and a construction with polynomial client memory matches this bound with a constant independent of $p,r,a$. We also separately bound the costs of reads and writes in this workload.
Lastly, public requests can in some cases be made cheaper by offloading their cost to preparation in earlier requests or cleanup in later ones. For both public reads and writes, we show localized tradeoffs constrained to a subset of requests, which demonstrate some of the limitations of such offloading.

item.title: The isodual constant of the LLL potential: exact values and structure
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2846
Authors: Nick Howgrave-Graham
Summary: The LLL potential $\Psi^2(B)=\prod_k\det\mathrm{Gram}(b_1,\dots,b_k)$, minimized over the bases of a lattice $L$ and normalized by its determinant, defines an isodual lattice invariant $\eta(L)$. Its supremum $\eta_n$ over $n$-dimensional lattices, introduced in ePrint 2007/105, is the staircase case of the generalized Hermite constants of Watanabe and Meyer, for which explicit values were known only for $n\le4$. We prove that $\eta_5=6$, attained only by $D_5$ and its dual: the flag analogue of Korkine and Zolotarev's value of $\gamma_5$. The natural reduction to four-dimensional lattices, through a function $\Phi_5$, does not suffice: the global maximum of $\Phi_5$ is $2^{16}/(3^4\cdot5^3)\approx6.4727$, attained not at $D_4$ but at an even $135$-modular lattice $M_*$, which we have not found in the literature. A second stage, over the lifts of the remaining region, completes the proof; both stages are computer-assisted, with about $9\times10^9$ leaves, each re-proved in interval arithmetic by a separately written checker; code and data are public. We also prove $\eta_8=2304$, attained by $E_8$, and show that $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$ and their duals are strict local maxima of $\eta$ (for $n=6,7$ these are the conjectured extremal lattices). Asymptotically, $\log\eta_n=(\frac14+o(1))\,n^2\log n$.
For lattice reduction we introduce the $\Psi$-Hermite constant $\mu_m$, the largest first Gram–Schmidt norm in a potential-minimal basis of an $m$-dimensional lattice, and bound it through $\eta_m$. This gives $\mu_m=\gamma_m$, Hermite's constant, for $m\le5$, and $\mu_m\le\exp(O(\log^2 m))$ in general.

item.title: On Composing Oracle Separations
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2845
Authors: Willy Quach, Felix Rohrbach
Summary: Black-box separations constitute very powerful technical barriers against constructing primitives from specific building blocks. However, they give surprisingly little indication on the usefulness of \emph{combining} several such building blocks in a single construction.
We propose a set of technical conditions, under which (fully) black-box separations compose with each other. That is, if two black-box separations $P_1 \stackrel{BB}{\nRightarrow} Q$ and $P_2 \stackrel{BB}{\nRightarrow} Q$ satisfy our conditions, then $Q$ is also separated from black-box combinations of $P_1$ and $P_2$. When applicable, these conditions can be established without unpacking the full technical details of the base separations.
As our main application, we show that combining indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) with collision resistant hash functions is unlikely to yield hard problems in the complexity class $SZK$, and thus unlikely to suffice for primitives such as lossy functions or fully homomorphic encryption. Previous lower bounds on iO only applied to combinations of iO with one-way permutations (Asharov-Segev, FOCS '15 and Bitansky-Degwekar-Vaikuntanathan, SIAM Journal on Computing '21).

item.title: Antipodal necessity for rotation symmetric bent functions of degree at most three
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2844
Authors: Filipe Martins Vono
Summary: The conjecture that every homogeneous rotation symmetric bent Boolean function has degree two remains open in general. We prove a necessary condition that settles the degree-three case of this conjecture. Let $n>0$ be even. If a rotation symmetric Boolean function of degree at most three in $n$ variables is bent, then its algebraic normal form contains the antipodal quadratic orbit $\sum_{i2} x_i x_{i+n2}$. A homogeneous cubic has no quadratic terms, so no homogeneous rotation symmetric cubic Boolean function is bent, in any even number of variables. The condition also applies to nonhomogeneous functions with arbitrary lower-degree terms compatible with rotation symmetry; it neither classifies these functions nor addresses degree four and higher. The proof uses only finite Fourier analysis and linear algebra over the binary field. Restriction to the fixed space of a rotation of odd order reduces the problem to a power-of-two number of variables. There, Parseval's identity and a rigidity property of rotation symmetric quadratic forms impose incompatible conditions on a single fiber of the function. A second proof replaces the final fiber argument by descent through a single unipotent Jordan block. Examples illustrate the hypotheses. A Lean formalization of the original proof is provided as supplementary material; the Jordan proof has not been formalized.

item.title: Adaptively Secure (Threshold) Batched IBE from Static Assumptions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2843
Authors: Sourav Das, Pratish Datta, Aditi Partap, Swagata Sasmal
Summary: Batched identity-based encryption (batched IBE) lets a key authority release one short decryption key for a set of identities and a batch label/epoch. It has been used to mitigate maximal extractable value (MEV) attacks on public blockchains. Existing constructions either use the generic-group and/or random-oracle models, or rely on $q$-type assumptions whose size grows with the batch-size bound.
In this paper, we present the first adaptively secure batched IBE scheme from static assumptions. Our scheme supports an exponential identity space and an exponential epoch space, and its ciphertexts, digests, and batch keys consist of a constant number of group elements independent of the batch size. Our scheme relies on composite-order bilinear groups, and we prove its adaptive security assuming hardness of static subgroup decision assumptions and a static pairing assumption, with a security loss polynomial in the security parameter $\lambda$ and the number of key queries. Our proof does not rely on $q$-type assumptions, random oracles, generic-group arguments, or complexity leveraging. We also present a threshold version with adaptive challenge security under static corruption, and translate our scheme to prime-order bilinear groups under the static MDDH assumption.

item.title: Enabling Memory Encryption Using Ascon Derivatives
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2842
Authors: Sergej Deutsch, Christoph Dobraunig, David Durham, Simon Johnson, Krystian Matusiewicz, Carlos Rozas, Alexander Tereschenko
Summary: Keeping data stored in memory confidential is a tough challenge when assuming an adversary with physical access to it. First, we have fine-grained access to typically 256 to 512 bits at once, so nonces or tags of the typical sizes used for authenticated encryption would lead to a sizeable overhead. Second, we have stringent performance requirements, including low latency that directly impacts CPU performance and, more generally, strict area and energy constraints, especially for the high bandwidth of memory interfaces. Currently, memory encryption solutions typically rely on the AES block cipher. In this paper, we explore ways of using Ascon as a building block for memory encryption. Our analysis shows that Ascon-based constructions achieve better performance than AES-based HCTR2 and can also compete with XTS-AES while providing larger block sizes.

item.title: SEC: One-Share Everywhere-Short Secret Sharing from Lossless Expanders
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2841
Authors: Muhammad Arzaki, Muhammed F. Esgin, Amin Sakzad, Ron Steinfeld
Summary: We introduce \(\mathsf{SEC}\), an expander-code-based ramp secret sharing scheme over \(\mathbb{Z}\)-modules, particularly suitable for lattice-based distributed cryptography. It is everywhere-short: bounded secret coefficients yield bounded share coefficients, and the integer reconstruction vectors have bounded entries. Moreover, each participant receives exactly one share, regardless of the number of parties and the privacy and reconstruction thresholds. This improves on prior schemes with bounded share coefficients and bounded entries in the integer reconstruction vectors, in which the number of sub-shares or shares per participant grows either with the number of parties and the threshold or with the security parameter. The construction rests on a coding-theoretic observation: in the bi-adjacency matrix of a lossless bipartite expander, unique-neighbor peeling completes every sufficiently small set of columns to a square unimodular submatrix. We prove correctness, everywhere-shortness, and linearity, and give a publicly computable entrywise bound on the reconstruction vector our algorithm returns for each authorized set. For privacy, we introduce hard-core local leakage resilience, which strengthens the leakage-resilience notion of Nielsen and Simkin (EUROCRYPT 2020) to protect a hard-core function of the secret, and we prove that \(\mathsf{SEC}\) satisfies it against correlated multi-query local leakage under the \(\mathsf{MatrixHint\text{-}MLWE}\) problem, which admits a reduction from the standard \(\mathsf{MLWE}\) problem. For \(n=60\) participants and security parameter \(\kappa = 128\), \(\mathsf{SEC}\) achieves privacy threshold \(6\) against \(2^{64}\) leakage queries and empirical reconstruction threshold \(46\). The ideal entropy-coded secret and share sizes are about \(3.5\) KiB and \(6.4\) KiB, respectively.

item.title: MPCTM: MPC-Based Trajectory Matching on Unmanned Autonomous Systems
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2840
Authors: Dominik Roy George, Martin Zbudila, Barry Van Leeuwen
Summary: Emerging technologies such as Unmanned Autonomous Systems (UASs) are increasingly being deployed across several application domains. Their deployment, however, introduces safety risks, especially when unmanned vehicles operate in shared operational spaces (e.g., air, land, or maritime) and may follow collision-prone paths. This creates the need for solutions that can detect possible collisions among pre-planned trajectories, thereby improving operational safety and reducing risk. At the same time, revealing trajectories in plaintext leaks sensitive information, such as traversal patterns, deployment and infrastructure locations, and potentially private user data. In this paper, we present a privacy-preserving trajectory matching protocol based on Multi-Party Computation (MPC). We introduce an end-to-end secure scheme for collision detection that reveals no information beyond the prescribed output. Our solution models the behaviour of UASs along their paths, accurately capturing collisions that may occur between discretely sampled points. We further propose a lightweight, MPC-friendly model and discuss the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency for the two approaches. We provide a proof-of-concept implementation of our scheme and compare it to the closest state-of-the-art solution. Our evaluation shows that our work MPCTM, in the dealer mode, improves the online latency upon previous work by over 2x in our modelled protocol and by 8x in our lightweight protocol. In autonomous mode, our protocol results in a slow-down of 2.5-3x, while providing a more expressive model with no false negatives and fully preserving privacy of the trajectory data.

item.title: Practical Confidential Clustering for Federated Learning using Efficient Secret-Sharing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2839
Authors: Cédric Prigent, Sonia Ben Mokhtar
Summary: Federated Learning (FL) often suffers from statistical heterogeneity, where diverging data distributions prevent a single global model from achieving high utility for all participants. Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses this problem by grouping similar clients to train personalized sub-models, yet performing such clustering while ensuring strict confidentially with minimal communication overhead remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces CCFL, a framework for Confidential Clustering that executes clustering logic, including distance computations and centroid updates, entirely within the encrypted domain using Replicated Secret Sharing (RSS). CCFL orchestrates a unified pipeline that integrates client-side feature extraction, an anonymization server for oblivious shuffling, and Multi-Party Computation (MPC)-based clustering to ensure both input privacy and participant unlinkability. By employing a ring-based Euclidean distance optimization, CCFL significantly reduces interactive rounds, achieving up to $46.7\times$ computational speedup under realistic LAN and WAN constraints. Our one-shot clustering approach decouples heavy cryptographic computation from the training loop, allowing the system to scale seamlessly to thousands of clients with negligible edge overhead. Finally, downstream evaluations confirm that CCFL achieves a superior privacy-utility trade-off, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art personalized FL paradigms without exposing sensitive feature geometries.

item.title: DKG: A Dual-Layer Knowledge Graph and LLM Co-Driven Framework for Fully Automated Side-Channel Analysis of Cryptosystems
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2838
Authors: Wenquan Zhou, An Wang, Yaoling Ding, Jiakun Li, Jingqi Zhang, Liehuang Zhu
Summary: Cryptographic algorithms underpin billions of devices, from payment smartcards to smartphone secure enclaves and industrial controllers. Yet their physical implementations risk leaking secret keys. Non-profiled side-channel analysis (SCA) evaluates whether such leakage enables key recovery, but executing it end-to-end remains expert-intensive. Large language model (LLM) agents now automate complex workflows across many domains, yet reliable key recovery requires specialized SCA knowledge that must be extracted and organized from scattered technical literature. In this paper, we propose DKG, a dual-layer knowledge graph and LLM co-driven key-recovery agent framework. We introduce the first graph schema designed specifically for SCA: an upper layer of configuration components and a lower layer of diagnostic strategies, joined by cross-layer relationships. An LLM-driven three-step extraction pipeline (Locate & Rewrite, Triple Extraction, and Knowledge Fusion) builds the graph from raw technical documents without manual annotation, and at runtime the retrieved knowledge drives a closed-loop autonomous attack workflow. Built from a corpus of 166 technical documents, the graph contains 1,334 entities and 1,813 relationships. On eight datasets covering AES, DES, and SM4 across smartcards, FPGAs, and MCUs, DKG with DeepSeek-V3.2 achieves a 97.5% end-to-end key-recovery success rate. By comparison, ReAct-RAG, a text-retrieval-augmented agent, achieves only 68.8%. Across the open-weights backbones DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5, and Qwen3.5, DKG achieves an average success rate of 93.3%. To the best of our knowledge, DKG is the first framework to achieve consistent end-to-end automated key recovery across diverse implementations. Its automated pipeline lets the graph grow with new literature, and its dual-layer organization provides a basis for extending DKG to additional SCA techniques.

item.title: Adaptive Leaky LWE and Its Security
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2837
Authors: Chuanqi Zhang, Muhammed F. Esgin, Ron Steinfeld
Summary: The Leaky LWE problem, proposed by Lai, Swarnakar, and Woo (CiC '25), studies whether LWE samples remain pseudorandom in the presence of noisy linear information about their secrets and errors. In Leaky LWE, the leakage matrix may depend on the public matrix, but must be chosen before the LWE challenge is revealed. We study $t$-round adaptive Leaky LWE, where each leakage matrix may depend on the challenge and all preceding leakage answers. Under explicit norm, smoothing, and sampling conditions, we reduce Gaussian-secret LWE to this problem at the corresponding source parameters for polynomially many rounds. The reduction preserves the public-matrix distribution and access to its correlated oracle, and supports rectangular leakage matrices and non-spherical discrete Gaussians over arbitrary orders in number fields.

item.title: Doubly-Efficient Private Information Retrieval from Modular Forms
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2836
Authors: Alexandra Henzinger, Seyoon Ragavan
Summary: We present new information-theoretic protocols for $s$-server, doubly-efficient private information retrieval (PIR) in sublinear server time and one extra bit of space on the servers, for every constant $s \geq 2$. On an $n$-bit database, each of the $s$ PIR servers first builds and stores a preprocessing data structure consisting of $n+1$ bits (which is unique to each server, and after which the server may discard the original database). Then, each server answers a PIR query in time $T_s(n)$, by reading at most $T_s$ bits of its data structure and sending them to the user.
In the two server setting ($s=2$), our PIR protocols achieve $T_2 = n^{0.82}$, matching the server time of the state-of-the-art schemes of Henzinger and Ragavan (EUROCRYPT 2026) while shrinking their storage from $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ to $n+1$ bits. With $s \geq 3$ servers, our PIR protocols retain the $n+1$ bits of storage and additionally improve on the server time of all prior information-theoretic $s$-server schemes with $n^{1+o(1)}$ storage: for example, achieving $T_3 = n^{0.74}$ and $T_{10} = n^{0.61}$ (previously $n^{0.79}$ and $n^{0.75}$). Asymptotically, as the server count $s$ grows, we shrink the number of servers required to achieve a given server-work exponent from $s^{3.9}$ to $s$.
Our results draw inspiration from matching-vector techniques (Efremenko, STOC 2009), which we generalize to handle degree-two computations in the exponent. Using this generalization, we build doubly-efficient PIR from the new intermediate abstraction of Fourier-sparse cone-delta functions. Then, we construct such Fourier-sparse cone-delta functions via a connection to modular forms and complex analysis: if a Fourier-sparse cone-delta function does not exist, then there exists a modular form which has too many roots, contradicting the valence formula.

item.title: Multi-Hop Functional Encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2835
Authors: Pratish Datta, Jiaxin Guan, Alexis Korb, Amit Sahai
Summary: In this paper, we initiate the study of multi-hop functional encryption ($\mathsf{MHFE}$), a new primitive for computing over encrypted data in recursive and multi-stage workflows while enabling controlled release of intermediate outputs. $\mathsf{MHFE}$ supports dynamic directed-acyclic computation graphs in which each node is labeled by a function and is equipped with a restricted secret key that reveals only that node's output, yet the computation can continue downstream on a forwardable encrypted state. In doing so, $\mathsf{MHFE}$ simultaneously overcomes (i) multi-hop fully homomorphic encryption's need for a globally trusted, always-online decryption key to reveal intermediate values, (ii) standard FE's lack of a native mechanism for forwarding reusable encrypted state across stages and handling evolving datasets without a fresh recomputation, and (iii) Multi Party Computation's deployment friction stemming from interaction and liveness/coordination requirements (at the cost of a central key-issuing authority).
We formalize $\mathsf{MHFE}$ security via the simulation paradigm extending standard FE collusion resistance to the multi-hop setting; this simulation-based notion captures the intended information flow in recursive computations most accurately by characterizing an adversary's entire view as simulatable given only the authorized intermediate outputs. Our security games impose a natural topological-order on queries: a hop key for a node may be requested only after the ciphertexts/keys on all incoming edges to that node have been fixed. We then give the first generic simulation-secure construction of public-key $\mathsf{MHFE}$ for all polynomial-size circuits from any IND-secure standard FE for circuits.

item.title: Undine: Distributed Extendable Merkle Tree Storage with Private Retrieval and Efficient Reconfiguration
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2834
Authors: Nicolas Alhaddad, Harry Eldridge, Julia Guskind, Eran Tromer, Mayank Varia
Summary: Clients of transparency logs, public-key directories, and shielded blockchain pools require authenticated access to an ever-changing Merkle tree, without storing it in full or revealing which entry they open. We seek to distribute storage and query work across independent servers as the data grows and participants join, leave, change their shares, or misbehave.
We present Undine, which combines a distributed Merkle tree encoding with private retrieval from independently-maintained fragments. Maintainers can choose and efficiently adjust the size of their stored fragments, to offer a flexible tradeoff against the number of maintainer replies needed for authenticated data reconstruction by clients. Maintainers can also perform authenticated updates and appends, at a write cost of just twice the number of modified Merkle nodes.
Undine uses a linear encoding of the Merkle tree nodes to divide evenly the storage and retrieval load across maintainers. This is combined with a private information retrieval (PIR) protocol that operates directly over the linearly-encoded fragments. Undine avoids repeated storage and computation for nodes shared by Merkle paths across records, producing the same PIR replies with work over tree values linear in the filled prefix. Record sizes adapt as the prefix grows to balance query and reply sizes.
Clients verify against the Merkle root, without commitments to individual PIR databases. Computational query privacy holds against any coalition. Undine is also secure against selective-failure leakage (i.e., deductions from acceptance), up to the PIR backend's correctness error, given enough timely honest replies, fixed public timing, and no reply-dependent follow-up.
We evaluate UndineLog, our append-only implementation of Undine combined with YPIR. On a height-50 sparse Merkle tree with a 4GiB prefix of nonempty 32-byte leaves and a reconstruction threshold of 64, a maintainer replies in 100ms (single-core); a client can process 192 replies from maintainers and reconstruct a verified opening in 380ms, even with 64 corrupted replies. Scaled up to 1TiB and 256 threshold , a maintainer answers in 1.13s. Existing shielded pools can use this service without consensus changes.

item.title: The Closest Vector Problem on Gadget Lattices: Efficient Algorithms and Voronoi Geometry
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2833
Authors: Daniele Micciancio
Summary: Gadget lattices are a prominent family of lattices widely used in lattice-based cryptography, error-correcting codes, and computational complexity. We present efficient algorithms for the Closest Vector Problem (CVP) on power and CRT gadget lattices and their duals, handling arbitrary real-valued target vectors.
For the parity-check power gadget lattice, we give a practical, deterministic O(n) linear-time exact CVP solver based on a new, specialized "deferred greedy" graph-cut technique. Through an explicit characterization of the Voronoi cell, we provide a comprehensive analysis of existing decoders: we prove that the standard BDD algorithm of Micciancio and Peikert (2012) unexpectedly solves CVP exactly for odd base b and integer targets, but degrades to a worst-case approximation factor of n^0.5 for binary base b=2 and continuous targets. Furthermore, we prove that standard pruned sphere decoding requires exponential time exp(Omega(n)) even when using a geometrically optimal basis.
For the dual (generator) power gadget lattice, we construct an obtuse superbasis---proving for the first time that it is a lattice of "Voronoi's first kind"---which yields a polynomial-time O(n^3) exact CVP algorithm via graph min-cut reductions. Geometrically, we determine all successive minima and enumerate the facets of their Voronoi cells. In particular, we show that while the parity-check lattice has a sparse Voronoi cell with n^2+n facets, the generator lattice reaches the theoretical upper bound of 2(2^n-1) facets. Finally, we observe that CRT gadget lattices and their duals admit an orthogonal basis, yielding trivial linear-time CVP algorithms.

item.title: An Agile Homomorphic Encryption and ML-KEM Scheme for Privacy-Preserving Health Data Processing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2832
Authors: Daniel RESENDE, Nadia El Mrabet, Ulrich Kühne
Summary: The storage and processing of health data raise serious privacy con- cerns; therefore, the data must be encrypted. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) allows computations on encrypted data, which makes it a very promising technology in this context. However, although the efficiency of FHE algorithms has improved in recent years, they remain very complex. The security of several prominent FHE schemes is based on variants of the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem, which is also the basis of Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), the new post-quantum standard for asymmetric encryption. In this paper, we propose an agile cryptographic scheme – combining ML-KEM and BGV – that allows efficient implementations in an embedded use case. We describe the parameter selection for the proposed scheme and show its feasibility with a proof-of-concept implementation.

item.title: Twisted Towers: Fully Costed Special Tower NFS Attacks on BLS12-381 and BN254
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2831
Authors: Gautam Botrel
Summary: BLS12-381 is commonly said to offer "126 bits" of security and BN254 "about 100 bits". Both figures are estimates of the special tower number field sieve (STNFS) in the target group $\mathbb{F}_{p^{12}}^*$, and both count abstract operations in models that leave out whole phases of the attack. We replace them by complete ledgers in which every step is priced in machine instructions: relation collection, cofactorisation, filtering, linear algebra, both individual logarithms and all failures. Under explicitly listed heuristics, a complete attack executes $2^{127.5}$ instructions for BLS12-381 and $2^{103.2}$ for the BN254 curve used in Ethereum, with success probability above $0.998$. For BLS12-381 this is $9.6$ bits below Pollard's rho on the curve counted the same way, where operation counts suggested one bit: the target group is clearly the weaker side. It is also $9.8$ bits below what the published design costs when it is completed with standard components and charged in full ($2^{137.3}$ instructions, level with rho). For BN254 our figure confirms the accepted level and gives it a concrete meaning.
The method rests on three ideas and on a systematic reduction of the work per sieved cell. First, a twisted tower: a unit $c$ of the sextic base field with $c\,\sigma(c)=-1$ turns the usual sign symmetry into a symmetry of order four that acts as a Frobenius power, so that relations and ideals come in orbits of four and the linear system has Gaussian-integer entries. Second, counting each relation once: coefficient-cube estimates count unit multiples of a relation as distinct; for the published BLS12-381 design only $2^{-2.8}$ of the counted relations are distinct, and we sieve a fundamental domain instead. Third, a sieve organised around reuse: only the harder side is sieved, tiny primes are handled by batch arithmetic, and the hits of a prime ideal are replayed from lists shared by all slices. A product-form linear algebra and a planned descent complete the method. Each technique is stated for a general special pair of tower shape $(6,2)$ and then instantiated on the two curves. Nothing was run at full size; the final designs assume up to $2^{112}$ bytes of storage, which the cost model does not charge; and the practical security of both curves is unchanged.

item.title: γ₁₁: Unequal Triangles and Adapted References — the macadamia 0050
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2849
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: This paper settles the ninth of the ten macadamias of the series on the Hermite constant in dimension 11: the perfect form $P$ = 0050:024468269 of rank 9, of determinant 8192/9 at minimum 4. The root paper reduces $\gamma_{11}$ to chains $L\supset M\supset N$ of lattices of ranks 11, 10, 9, each with minimum at least 4; we prove that every admissible chain whose rank-9 member is admissibly marked by $P$ has $\det L\ge 972$. No argument at rank 10 can do this, because an actual lattice of rank 10 with determinant $3328/3<4\cdot 972^{9/11}$ lies over $P$. The proof is computer-assisted, with explicit finite checks. Its decisive step is elementary: the three additive dual vectors of a section covector and the first normal usually have different lengths, and keeping the three lengths in the circle obstruction, instead of their maximum, gives a determinant cap that sharpens every subsequent contact and spectral bound. Adapted reference forms turn the contact conditions into exact rational tests, a common slack is retained throughout, and four computational results reduce the problem to a five-parameter root, exhausted by a finite cover of 6 993 terminal regions replayed in exact arithmetic.

item.title: γ₁₁: One Selected Contact, Two Linked Blocks — the macadamia 0030
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2830
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: This paper is one of five companion papers completing the proof of $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$ announced in the root paper and assembled in “A Focus on Hermite Constant 11”. The root paper reduces a lattice of rank 11 with minimum 4 and determinant below 972 to a chain of sections of ranks 11, 10 and 9 whose rank-9 member is admissibly marked by one of 4 487 813 perfect forms; ten of them, the macadamias, lie under an actual lattice of rank 10 and need proofs of their own. We settle the first, the form 0030:030301719 of $\Lambda_9$ under $\Lambda_{10}$, where the bound has little margin. The argument selects one contact of the reference lattice from the actual metric, keeps the off-diagonal column shared by two eight-dimensional blocks of the section metric, applies one determinant–trace theorem to both blocks, and closes with a rational cover of three scalar parameters. The proof is computer-assisted: its finite inputs are three outer-range covers, two middle-range covers with 10 498 and 1 140 leaves, an annulus tree with 3 567 leaves and four smaller trees, every leaf checked in exact rational arithmetic.

item.title: γ₁₁: Reduction by Sections — the macadamias 0019 and 0017
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2829
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: The root paper of this series reduces the value $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$ of the Hermite constant in dimension 11 to a statement about chains $L\supset M\supset N$ of lattices of ranks 11, 10 and 9 whose rank-9 member lies over one of 4 487 813 perfect forms of rank 9; the $\gamma_{11}$ paper settles all of them but ten, the macadamias. This paper settles two of the ten: 0019:030884313 (the form $P_S$ of the root paper, an extension of $E_8$ by a simplex vector) and 0017:001746552 (the form $P_K$, KAPPA9.2). We prove that every admissible chain whose rank-9 member is admissibly marked by the form has $\det L\ge 972$. The method is a reduction by sections: for 0019 the nine simplex contacts turn the problem into one about an eight-dimensional covariance matrix, and a tree of 17 347 nodes with 7 743 scalar determinant witnesses covers the remaining box; for 0017 a two-vector flag bound and the decomposition of the section metric along a short-dual plane and its rank-seven kernel reduce the problem to five parameters, covered by a tree of 3 010 595 nodes. The proof is computer-assisted: every finite check is stated as a Computational result, and the verification records in the certificate archive are named.

item.title: γ₁₁: A Finite Spectral Relaxation — the macadamia 0008
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2828
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: The root paper of this series reduces $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$ to a statement about chains of lattices $L\supset M\supset N$ of ranks 11, 10 and 9, cut along shortest dual vectors, whose rank-9 member lies over one of 4 487 813 perfect forms. Ten of these forms, the macadamias, lie under an actual lattice of rank 10 of small determinant and need a proof at rank 11, where the bound 972 is attained. This paper settles the form 0008:022143116, which lies under a section of $K_{11}$ with 276 minimal vectors: every admissible chain whose rank-9 member is admissibly marked by this form has $\det L\ge 972$. In coordinates aligned with the form, the section metric is $S=I+E$ with three blocks of size three. Two sufficient flag tests come from short dual covectors and integral triangles; local reductions, proved from rational comparisons and Bernstein or Sturm certificates, remove explicit regions of the parameters; every remaining real spectrum is mapped, with explicit allowances, into a finite relaxation on 81 grid nodes, which a tree of 400 nodes with 1 091 rational certificates, replayed in two exact arithmetic implementations, excludes. The proof is computer-assisted, with explicit finite checks stated as one Computational result.

item.title: γ₁₁: Contact Geometry — the macadamias 0001, 0014, 0059 and 0015
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2827
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: The root paper of this series reduces the value $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$ of the Hermite constant to a statement about chains of lattices $L\supset M\supset N$ of ranks 11, 10 and 9 whose rank-9 member lies, in the sense of Voronoi, over one of 4 487 813 perfect forms; the $\gamma_{11}$ paper excludes all of them but ten, the macadamias. This paper settles four macadamias, the forms 0001:010488327, 0014:001749549, 0059:016902802 and 0015:030291998, by one method: the geometry of the contacts of the form. A section frame of short dual vectors forces the first gluing of $M$ over $N$ to lie near one of finitely many coherent centres; at such a centre the rank-10 metric is compared with an explicit reference lattice, whose Delaunay cells and contact identities give a uniform bound on its covering radius; and a primitive-extension inequality turns that bound into $\det L\ge 972$. The proof is computer-assisted: every finite check it uses is stated as a Computational result with the records of the certificate archive that certify it, and all comparisons are between explicit rational numbers.

item.title: A Focus on Hermite Constant 11
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2826
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: This paper assembles the dimension-eleven argument in a series on the Hermite constants in dimensions ten, eleven and twelve. The root paper reduces a hypothetical lattice of minimum 4 and determinant below 972 to a chain of sections of ranks eleven, ten and nine. Its rank-nine section is marked by a perfect form below an explicit determinant cutoff. The global finite computation leaves 4 487 813 candidate forms and excludes all but ten by certificates. We state the mathematical content of these certificates, describe their data and checking rules, and prove why every valid certificate excludes the corresponding form. The four formats are trace, domain, glue and tree certificates; each tree must cover its entire stated domain. One of the ten remaining cases, 0052:005247066, is treated here by a complete gluing cover. Five companion papers settle the other nine. We also prove the common inequalities used by those local arguments. The resulting bound is $\gamma_{11}=4/\sqrt[11]{972}$, conditional on the attributed rank-nine classification, the rank-ten census and the stated global and local finite checks.

item.title: The Hermite Constants in Dimensions 10, 11 and 12
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2825
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: This paper introduces a series of seven papers establishing $\gamma_{10}^{10}=4^{10}/768$, $\gamma_{11}^{11}=4^{11}/972$ and $\gamma_{12}=4/\sqrt{3}$, under the attributed classification of perfect forms of rank nine and the explicitly stated computational inputs. The argument treats the dimensions in order. In dimension ten, a section orthogonal to a shortest dual vector is compared with a perfect form. A completed exact census leaves three possible reference forms, and matrix inequalities exclude a determinant below 768 in each case. In dimension eleven, two successive sections give a chain of ranks eleven, ten and nine. The dimension-ten bound controls the determinant of the last section. The verified global census and preliminary certificates reduce the problem to ten local cases: nine are treated in five companion papers, and one in “A Focus on Hermite Constant 11”. The local arguments combine contact geometry, section bounds and finite rational covers. Mordell’s inequality then gives the dimension-twelve upper bound, matched by the Coxeter–Todd lattice. We prove the common reduction, explain the dependency between the papers, and state exactly which finite assertions must be checked. The accompanying Lean development verifies the complete analytic deduction from those inputs; external exact checkers verify the large certificate data.

item.title: Incrementally Verifiable Oracle Aided Computation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2824
Authors: Shafi Goldwasser, Yael Tauman Kalai
Summary: Incrementally verifiable computation ($\IVC$) allows a prover to maintain a short proof that can be efficiently updated after each computation step, without retaining or recomputing the preceding execution. In the context of AI safety, the need for incremental verification is particularly important, as AI systems interact with users over time and perform further computation after each interaction. However, standard $\IVC$ schemes do not directly address a crucial feature of AI tasks: their dependence on external information and expertise. Indeed, the UK AISI Alignment Team~\cite{IrvingM25} emphasizes that verification methods for AI safety should accommodate access to external information and human judgment. This is the topic of this paper.
We construct $\IVC$ schemes for {\em oracle-aided} computations under the Learning with Errors ($\LWE$) assumption by first constructing succinct non-interactive arguments ($\SNARG$s), and then extending them to the incremental setting. We consider the following two settings, where below, $\lambda$ is the security parameter, $n$ is the input length, and $T$, $S$, and $Q$ are the time, space, and oracle-query bounds. \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Robust computations.} For bounded-space computations, including non-deterministic computations, in which every accepting purported execution on a false input contains at least an $\varepsilon$-fraction of incorrect oracle answers, we construct {\em privately verifiable} $\SNARG$s and $\IVC$. For $\IVC$, the corresponding robustness condition is imposed on the claimed configuration. Public parameters, private verification keys, and proofs have length $\poly(\lambda,S,\log T,1/\varepsilon)$, and verification uses $O(\lambda/\varepsilon)$ oracle calls. We complement this result with a lower bound ruling out (deterministic) publicly verifiable $\SNARG$s and $\IVC$s with public parameters of length $o(n)$, and $o(Q)$ verifier oracle queries.
\item \textbf{Signed oracles.} For oracles that digitally sign their query-answer pairs, we construct publicly verifiable $\SNARG$s and $\IVC$ without a robustness assumption, and with oracle-free setup and verification. Public parameters and proofs have length $\poly(\lambda,S,\log T)$. For deterministic computations with oracle query and answer lengths $\poly(\lambda,\log T)$, we remove the dependence on $S$, obtaining public parameter and proof lengths $\poly(\lambda,\log T)$.
\end{itemize} All our constructions have adaptive completeness and soundness. Sub-exponential hardness of $\LWE$ suffices for all constructions; polynomial hardness suffices in the deterministic signed-oracle setting when $T$ is polynomially bounded in $\lambda$. All cryptographic assumptions are required to hold even given access to the underlying oracle.

item.title: Revisiting the Security of OleF, t-OleF, and OlÆF
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2823
Authors: Tingting Guo, Peng Wang, Shuping Mao, Yan Jia, Jiadong Han
Summary: We revisit the security of OleF, t-OleF, and OlÆF and identify two independent security flaws. First, we establish a mask-compensation relation between continuation and termination processing in OleF and t-OleF. Exploiting this relation, we construct a two-encryption-query distinguisher against OleF with advantage $1 − 2^{−2n}$ . We further give two concrete AXU hash families for which the same attack applies to t-OleF, revealing flaws in the original DOSPRP and SPRTOP security proofs. We extend these attacks to OlÆF through valid encodings, breaking its privacy and integrity. In particular, the integrity forgery succeeds with probability 1 under full-domain verification when the target expansion length is 1 and extends to larger expansion lengths under suffix-only verification. Second, we refute the claimed ideal RUP integrity bound for variable-expansion online authenticated encryption. Even with an ideal tweakable online permutation, prior unverified decryption queries at smaller expansion lengths can reveal part of the target authentication suffix. We construct counterexamples showing that a single unverified decryption query or a single non-target verification query, followed by one forgery attempt, achieves a success probability of $3/8$, exceeding the claimed bound of $1/4$. We also derive generalized expressions for the forgery success probabilities of both attacks. Finally, we discuss the corresponding repair requirements.

item.title: Threshold Batched Attribute-Based Encryption from Succinct LWE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2822
Authors: Shayeef Murshid, Ramprasad Sarkar, Mriganka Mandal
Summary: Batched identity-based encryption (BIBE) enables a single compact key to decrypt ciphertexts associated with a designated batch of identities. Batched attribute-based encryption (B-ABE) extends this functionality to attribute-based access control, while threshold batched attribute-based encryption (TB-ABE) further distributes the decryption capability among multiple parties. Existing constructions of TB-ABE rely on bilinear pairings, motivating post-quantum alternatives. In this work, we give, to the best of our knowledge, the first lattice-based candidate construction of TB-ABE. Our construction combines the succinct polynomial-digest mechanism underlying lattice-based BIBE with key-homomorphic evaluation for arithmetic-circuit policies and linear secret sharing. We prove security under the ℓ-succinct LWE assumption, assuming the required share-uniformity property of the underlying ramp threshold sharing scheme.

item.title: Designing Quantum-Safe Network Architectures via Certified Randomness Distribution
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2821
Authors: Filip-Ioan Ceară, Diana Maimuţ
Summary: We propose an alternative design for quantum-safe network architectures, based on distributing certified randomness generated by different trust-level QRNGs. Our modular methodology aggregates high-trust entropy from upper network layers with local contributions, enhancing the security guarantees of locally available random sequences. Leveraging the physical guarantees of QRNGs and symmetric-key cryptographic algorithms for node authentication, our approach enables immediately deployable, quantum-safe infrastructures. Such a paradigm bypasses the practical security limitations of current QKD-based solutions, while avoiding massive key sizes and latency inherent to asymmetric PQC implementations.

item.title: The Minimum Bucket Capacity for Reliable Path ORAM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2820
Authors: Yijia Chang, Man Ho Au
Summary: Path ORAM hides memory access patterns by storing $N$ data blocks in a binary tree whose buckets have capacity $Z$, using a client-side stash for blocks that cannot be placed in the tree. Smaller buckets reduce storage and communication costs but increase the risk of stash overflow. The revised Path ORAM analysis in 2014 established an exponentially decreasing stash overflow probability for $Z \geq 5$. Experiments suggest small stashes at $Z=4$ and substantially larger ones at $Z=3$. However, it remained unknown whether $Z=4$ admits a uniform exponential stash bound or whether such a bound is impossible at $Z=3$.
We establish a sharp threshold at $Z=4$ for binary Path ORAM with tree depth $L=\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$. For $Z=4$, we prove that, uniformly over all database sizes and fixed access sequences, the stash size $S$ after the final refill satisfies \[ \Pr[S>R] \leq \frac{23}{28}\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^R \] for every integer $R \geq 0$. For $Z=3$, we exhibit a family of instances on which a single sequential scan of all $N$ blocks produces a stash of size $\Omega(N)$ with probability bounded away from zero. Thus, four is the minimum bucket capacity admitting a uniform exponential stash bound: a logarithmic stash suffices for polynomial-length executions with inverse-polynomial failure probability at $Z=4$, whereas at $Z=3$ no sublinear stash can make the overflow probability vanish uniformly.
Our proofs connect the actual Path ORAM process with dependent node loads to an auxiliary model with independent geometric node loads. This independence enables a recursive analysis of overflow that avoids the union bound over rooted subtrees used in the previous $Z=5$ proof. The main challenge is to transfer bounds from the auxiliary model to the actual process, which requires different techniques for the upper and lower bounds. For $Z=4$, we develop a two-stage randomization argument that bounds the actual process's exponential overflow moment by that of the auxiliary model. For $Z=3$, we develop a local continuous-time approximation with controlled errors that transfers an overflow surplus from the auxiliary model to the actual process, yielding the linear stash lower bound. Together, these arguments establish the sharp threshold at bucket capacity four.

item.title: How to Revoke Users in Encryption Schemes?
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2819
Authors: Sanjam Garg, Dimitris Kolonelos, Benjamin Ostrovsky, Guru-Vamsi Policharla
Summary: Revocation is essential for keeping encryption secure as keys leak, devices are compromised or users leave the system. We revisit the problem of revocation for encryption schemes and give, to our knowledge, the first approach combining anonymous, collusion-resistant revocation with unchanged keys and access rules, succinct ciphertext overhead and a trustless revocation authority, i.e. that cannot decrypt. Revoking a user publishes one random-looking pseudonym, without telling encryptors whose key was revoked. A party can decrypt future ciphertexts only if it is unrevoked and satisfies the original access decryption rule.
Our core observation is that revocation is, at heart, witness encryption for the statement that one satisfies the access rule and that the pseudonym bound to one's key has not been revoked. Although general-purpose witness encryption remains far from practical, we observe that the statements arising from revocation are simple and algebraic, and we show that they fall within the special-purpose framework of Garg et al. (CRYPTO 2025), which compiles short arguments of knowledge (called ``gadgets'') into efficient witness encryption using bilinear groups. Our technical contribution is a pair of succinct non-membership gadgets for this framework, one for a single hidden pseudonym and one that certifies non-revocation jointly for all users selected by an access rule. Both gadgets are generic and modular, as they compose with the gadgets expressing a wide range of access rules, and thus provide a single revocation mechanism that is designed once and reused across different encryption schemes, without redesigning either the scheme or the revocation.
These gadgets yield the following applications. First, we give a black-box transformation adding revocation to arbitrary independently instantiated public-key encryption, with constant-size cryptographic ciphertext overhead. For unrevoked users, confidentiality continues to rely only on the security of the underlying scheme. Then, we demonstrate applications to advanced encryption scheme, constructing revocable schemes for distributed broadcast, registered attribute-based, and registered threshold encryption, with succinct cryptographic ciphertext components and threshold decryption shares. We prove adaptive security of our schemes in the generic bilinear-group and random-oracle models.

item.title: Round-Optimal Statistical Verifiable Secret Sharing with Polynomial Complexity
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2818
Authors: Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Elisaweta Masserova
Summary: Verifiable secret sharing (Chor, Goldwasser, Micali, and Awerbuch; FOCS'85) is a central primitive in secure computation, and its round complexity has been studied extensively.
Rabin and Ben-Or [STOC'89] established the feasibility of statistical security up to $t2$ corruptions, and Patra, Choudhary, Rabin, and Rangan [Crypto'09] showed that three sharing rounds are necessary. The work of Applebaum, Kachlon and Patra [STOC'23] introduced the first round-optimal VSS with three rounds of sharing and one round for reconstruction, albeit with exponential communication in the number of parties.
We give the first round-optimal statistical VSS that has polynomial communication and computation for $t2$. This resolves the efficiency question left open by Applebaum, Kachlon and Patra. The protocol is obtained from a new notion of weak secret sharing, in which the reconstruction-time freedom of a corrupt dealer is limited to choosing verification keys, which is of independent interest.

item.title: From Degree Three to Degree Two: Statistical Randomized Encodings for All Functions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2817
Authors: Emmanuela Orsini, Arpita Patra
Summary: A randomized encoding represents a function by a simpler randomized map whose output allows recovery of the function value while revealing essentially no further information about the input. Perfectly correct and perfectly private encodings of degree three over $\F_2$ are known for every Boolean function, but degree two cannot provide these guarantees for all functions (Ishai and Kushilevitz, FOCS 2000 and ICALP 2002). Whether degree two suffices when small statistical errors are allowed in both correctness and privacy has remained open.
We construct quadratic randomized encodings of every Boolean function with exponentially small correctness and statistical privacy errors. The degree bound holds jointly in the input bits and independent uniform random bits, and the construction, encoder, decoder and simulator have complexity polynomial in the total size of mod-2 branching programs computing the function's output bits and in the security parameter. Our encodings also achieve decomposability and output locality three, meaning that each encoded bit depends on at most three input and random bits. These results resolve the degree-two and locality-three questions for statistical randomized encodings (Ishai, 2013). As an application, we obtain one-way functions of optimal output locality three from one-way functions in polynomial-time uniform $\mathrm{NC}^1$, improving the previous locality-four result under the same assumption (Applebaum, Ishai and Kushilevitz, FOCS 2004).
We also obtain quadratic multiparty randomized encodings with negligible correctness and statistical privacy errors against semi-honest corruption of any coalition of parties. Previous general constructions for $k\ge4$ parties provided perfect correctness and privacy against at most $\lfloor 2k/3\rfloor$ corruptions (Applebaum, Ishai, Karni and Patra, CRYPTO 2022). Through known reductions, our encodings yield non-interactive reductions of every functionality to a fixed three-party functionality and three-round protocols in the two-round OT-hybrid model, with negligible correctness and statistical privacy errors against every coalition. They also yield non-interactive client--server protocols for every function whenever a majority of the servers is honest, even when corrupted servers collude with any set of clients. This server threshold is optimal in this model when privacy is required against arbitrary client coalitions.

item.title: SoK: Understanding Virtual Machines over Fully Homomorphic Encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2816
Authors: Song Bian, Ziwei Ma, Yunhao Fu, Haowen Pan, Ruiyu Shen, Zhou Zhang, Ran Mao, Zaidong Li, Yintai Sun, Ruoyi Li, Zhenyu Guan
Summary: We survey the current literature on fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) from a virtual machine (VM) perspective. We observe that programs behave in an intrinsically different way over FHE than on plaintext, forming a new paradigm of computation that is fundamentally constrained by the obliviousness of data. To better understand the computational properties, we compile more than 125 works to formulate a cross-layer systematic view of FHE VMs, with a special focus on understanding the concrete programming models over encrypted data. In particular, we identify three distinct forms of VMs over FHE, namely, the SISD VM, the SIMD VM, and the hybrid VM. To aid the cross-layer systematization, we also discuss how current FHE compilers and hardware accelerators can be applied to enhance the usability and performance of the respective VMs. In the experiment, we test eight VM instructions with varying precision as well as two end-to-end application programs to quantitatively assess the concrete design trade-offs for each of the VM paradigms. We conclude that FHE VMs of different types exhibit distinct utility and performance characteristics, necessitating new design methodologies to be developed in a cross-layer manner.

item.title: Jazzline: Composable CryptoLine Functional Correctness Proofs for Jasmin Programs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2815
Authors: José Bacelar Almeida, Manuel Barbosa, Gilles Barthe, Lionel Blatter, Gustavo Delerue, João Diogo Duarte, Benjamin Gregoire, Tiago Oliveira, Miguel Quaresma, Pierre-Yves Strub, Ming-Hsien Tsai, Bow-Yaw Wang, Bo-Yin Yang
Summary: Jasmin is a programming language for high-speed and high-assurance cryptography. Correctness proofs of Jasmin programs are typically carried out deductively in EasyCrypt. This allows generality, modularity and composable reasoning, but does not scale well for low-level architecture-specific routines. CryptoLine offers a semi-automatic approach to formally verify algebraically-rich low-level cryptographic routines. CryptoLine proofs are self-contained: they are not integrated into higher-level formal verification developments. This paper shows how to soundly use CryptoLine to discharge subgoals in functional correctness proofs for complex Jasmin programs. We extend Jasmin with annotations and provide an automatic translation into a CryptoLine model, where most complex transformations are certified. We also formalize and implement the automatic extraction of the semantics of a CryptoLine proof

item.title: Registration-based Encryption with Logarithmic Registration
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2814
Authors: Xingfu Yan, Guiqiu Liao, Fan Yang, Haining Yang, Zheng Gong, Fucai Luo, Bowen Zhao
Summary: Registration-based encryption (RBE) preserves IBE's identity-only encryption interface while eliminating key escrow: users generate their own keys, and a Key Curator manages only registered public keys. However, this design introduces a new challenge: user registration, since every joining user rrequires KC to update the registry. Although theoretical RBE constructions achieve polylogarithmic registration, they rely on costly cryptographic techniques and remain impractical. In existing deployable black-box RBE, registration takes $O(\sqrt{N})$ time ($N$ denotes the maximum user capacity). This gap between theoretical registration efficiency and deployability makes registration a key performance bottleneck for large-scale deployments of pairing-based RBE.
This work presents a black-box pairing-based RBE construction under the decisional $(R,S,T,f)$-Diffie-Hellman assumption. Build on the multilinear tree, when registering a user's public key, KC updates only the corresponding root-to-leaf path associated with the user. Therefore, registration in our construction takes $O(\log \sqrt{N})$ time for the maximum user capacity $N$. Moreover, we provides membership and non-membership verification, and their batch verification supports to check registration status of multiple users. Experiments show registration and key generation complete in milliseconds when $N=10^7$. Compared with Glaeser et al. (CCS'23), our scheme accelerates registration by up to \(158\times\) and key generation by up to \(230\times\) with practical overheads.

item.title: Overcoming Padding in Cryptography via Hardness of Certifying Random Strings
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2813
Authors: Yao-Ching Hsieh, Abhishek Jain, Jiatu Li, Surya Mathialagan
Summary: Modern cryptography relies on a provable security paradigm where the security of a primitive is established from the intractability of one or more computational problems. Hybrid arguments are central to this approach. Somewhat unexpectedly, many security proofs in the literature that use this methodology require hybrids with description-size larger than the real scheme. To argue security, the real scheme is artificially padded to match this size. This so-called “superfluous padding” phenomenon is surprisingly commonplace and poses a barrier to achieving succinct cryptographic primitives where the size of the scheme parameters does not grow with the input length.
We present a framework to eliminate padding in cryptography. We demonstrate several applications, including rate-1 iO, succinct (and extractable) witness encryption and succinct non-interactive arguments with short CRS for subclasses of NP, and multi-input functional encryption for functions with unbounded arity.
To obtain our results, we establish a new connection between cryptography and proof complexity. Central to our approach is the notion of proof-complexity generators (PCGs) [Krajíček'01, Alekhnovich, Ben-Sasson, Razborov, Wigderson'04], which, informally speaking, formalizes the hardness of certifying random (incompressible) strings with propositional proof systems. Our applications are derived from a master theorem that lifts cryptographic security on “compressible instances” to security on any instance under the existence of PCGs. Due to its broad scope, this theorem might find future application

item.title: Constructions of Boolean Correctors with Optimal Nonlinearity and Vectorial Correctors Beyond Optimal Linear Correction Order
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2812
Authors: Zhaole Li, Deng Tang
Summary: Correctors are postprocessing functions that reduce or eliminate statistical bias in raw bitstreams produced by physical noise sources in true random number generators. In this paper, we develop a framework based on binary Krawtchouk polynomials for analyzing and constructing Boolean and vectorial correctors. This framework reformulates the Walsh-layer criterion into finite moment constraints on support-layer counts and preimage-layer counts. We also establish universal upper bounds on the nonlinearity of correctors, and necessary conditions on the achievable correction order. For Boolean functions, we prove that $(n-1)$-correctors are either the parity function or its complement. Then we characterize the support-layer profiles of $(n-2)$- and $(n-3)$-correctors and establish upper bounds on nonlinearity. For $n=2^k\ge 8$, a self-addressing construction yields $(n-2)$-correctors achieving the optimal nonlinearity $2^{n-1}-2^{n-1}/n$ with resiliency $n/2-2$ and algebraic degree $k+1$. Notably, this provides the first known infinite family of nonlinear correctors achieving both optimal correction order and optimal nonlinearity for that order, while having a resiliency strictly lower than the correction order. Furthermore, using constant-weight addressing, we construct $(n-d-1)$-correctors that asymptotically meet the nonlinearity upper bounds for every fixed $d\ge 1$. Our profile characterization also reveals inherent limitations of injective Maiorana--McFarland constructions at correction order $n-3$. For vectorial functions, we construct nonlinear $(s(2^m-1),m,s2^{m-1}+\ell-1)$-correctors for every $m\ge 2$ under certain conditions on $s$ and $\ell$, with resiliency at most $s2^{m-1}-2$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first infinite family of nonlinear correctors whose correction order simultaneously exceeds that of optimal linear corrector and its own resiliency. Finally, we introduce a secondary construction that lifts these vectorial correctors to larger input dimensions while preserving their correction-order advantage. This approach yields a nonlinearity of $2^{n-1}-2^{n-n_0-1}$, where $n_0$ is the input dimension of the base corrector, along with explicit resiliency and a flexible algebraic degree.

item.title: More Keys, Less Commitment: Key-Committing Attacks on BBB Accordions via Encode-then-Encipher and a Key-Committing Transform
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2811
Authors: Donghoon Chang, Yukihito Hiraga, Yusuke Naito, Yu Sasaki, Takeshi Sugawara
Summary: Cryptographic accordions with beyond-birthday-bound (BBB) security are being actively studied in connection with NIST’s ongoing standardization effort. We show that BBB security of an accordion does not necessarily strengthen key commitment of AE built from it: in many BBB accordions, additional keys introduced for BBB security give an adversary extra degrees of freedom. Exploiting this observation, we present $O(1)$ key-committing attacks on a broad range of AE schemes built from BBB accordions, mostly via the Encode-then-Encipher (EtE) paradigm, including CHCTR2, eCTR-based accordions, THCTR, HCTR+, TCT2, and bbb-ddd-AES under a natural polynomial-hash instantiation. To address this issue, we propose CACH, a black-box transform from BBB-secure accordions to robust AE (RAE) with key-committing security. CACH achieves BBB multi-user RAE security and achieves $t/2$-bit key-committing security with a $t$-bit tag for $n \le t \le 2n$ in the ideal-cipher model. CACH uses only AES-based components and supports all AES key sizes, making it compatible with NIST’s design goals. We instantiate CACH with CHCTR2. CACH-CHCTR2 with AES-256 outperforms EtE-HCTR2 with Rijndael-256 and EtE-CHCTR2 for short messages.

item.title: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2810
Authors: Maksym Ioffe, Dahlia Malkhi
Summary: We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of hash-based, post-quantum-secure protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. QUASI produces attestations that reduce the size and verification cost to a fraction of a full hash-based signatures collection, without relying on SNARKs or a trusted setup.
QUASI rests on a surprising discovery: each party need not sign the entire statement. Authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for a quorum to attest to the whole. We turn this insight into a randomized construction that achieves reductions of more than 10x in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures.
QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Operationally, QUASI requires no additional interactive setup or preprocessing beyond independent key generation by parties for the underlying hash-based authentication scheme. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI’s savings with succinct-proof compression.

item.title: Pastel: Single Secret Leader Election with Private Weights
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2809
Authors: Jung Hee Cheon, Kevin Choi, Intak Hwang, Jaehee Kang, Alireza Kavousi, Junho Lee, Yongdong Yeo
Summary: A single secret leader election (SSLE) protocol allows an election of exactly one leader among $n$ parties in a secrecy-preserving manner, where only the elected leader knows it has won until it publicly announces and claims leadership. Motivated by proof-of-stake blockchains where stakes are stored in an encrypted or committed form for the sake of privacy, we design and implement the first SSLE protocol with private weights. Each party's probability of winning an election in our protocol is weighted by stake, and these weights are private. Prior schemes in the literature only allow probabilistic (i.e. expectation of one but can be zero or many leaders) elections in the same setting.
Preserving privacy also means public verification is paramount in order for a protocol to be practically reliable. In this respect, our protocol achieves security against malicious adversaries with a concrete implementation. In particular, we concretely implement the needed zero-knowledge proofs and thus do not rely on slashing (financial penalties) to achieve end-to-end malicious security, though slashing can still serve as a performance optimization. Along the way, we observe that previous SSLE protocols in a setting without private weights (either unweighted or with public weights) are either maliciously secure with implementation or post-quantum secure but not both, while our protocol achieves both.

item.title: An improved algorithm to solve the isogeny problem in dimension 2 with precomputation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2808
Authors: Maria Corte-Real Santos
Summary: We give a new algorithm for the superspecial isogeny problem in dimension $2$. After a one-time precomputation depending only on $p$ (which succeeds with overwhelming probability), each instance is solved in expected time and memory $p^{3/4+o(1)}$. This result is unconditional, relying on no heuristics. Including the precomputation, a single instance is solved in time $p^{19/23+o(1)}$, improving on the $p^{1+o(1)}$ of the Costello-Smith algorithm. The improvement holds even with the same memory as (the rigorous version of) their algorithm.
The key ingredient is an algorithm that computes the equations of the Humbert surfaces $\mathcal{H}_{N^2}$ modulo $p$ for all $N$ up to a bound $D$ growing with $p$. These equations give a membership test for optimally $(N,N)$-split surfaces, which we evaluate in batches using fast multipoint evaluation. This speeds up the bottleneck of the Costello-Smith algorithm: finding an isogeny from a superspecial principally polarised abelian surface to a product of supersingular elliptic curves.

item.title: FirstSwap: Pre-Consensus Trade Approvals for Decentralized Market Design
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2807
Authors: William Diamond, Fatima Elsheimy, Dahlia Malkhi, Geoff Ramseyer, Srivatsan Sridhar
Summary: Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering.
